name: Epic Fantasy
brief: A heroic, wide-open orchestral cue in a modal key. The colour comes from dorian and mixolydian: the raised sixth of dorian and the flat seventh of mixolydian give it an old-world, open sound without leaning on a minor-key cliche. A horn calls first, a harp figure rolls underneath, choir-style pads hold the chords, and an ostinato bass keeps the stride. The key contrast is legato against staccato: long singing lines in the horn and strings against short, crisp woodwind and string figures. Original fanfares only. Tempo 80 to 130, default 108.
neverDo: Quote or paraphrase a known fantasy theme or fanfare.
Stay on one articulation; legato lines and staccato figures must both appear.
Leave the mode to a plain major or minor scale for more than a few bars.
Over-orchestrate every bar; let the horn call and the harp figure stand alone for a phrase.
Use an unlicensed sample or a leaked library.

bass.approach: Low strings and bass drum on an ostinato that walks the root and fifth in steady eighths, lifting to the sixth at phrase ends.

voicings: Open fifths and fourths in the horns
Harp arpeggios in the raised-sixth mode, spread across two octaves
Sustained choir-style pads on root, fifth and ninth

habits: Open with a single horn call over a quiet harp figure.
Answer a legato phrase with a staccato one, and swap them on the repeat.
Lift to a mixolydian chord at the high point, then fall back to the dorian centre.
Finish on an open fifth, not a full triad.

listeningNotes: A horn call states a modal tune in dorian, with a mixolydian lift at the high point.
Legato sections (long lines) and staccato sections (short figures) both appear, and the loudness and note density differ between them.
A harp-style arpeggio figure runs under the call.
Pads hold the chords and an ostinato bass keeps the stride.
The fanfare is original and ends on an open fifth.
